sources.title: Canva vs Figma: A Practitioner's 2026 Take
sources.content:
Canva vs Figma: Where the Handoff Actually Sits
Canva and Figma are not two answers to the same question. Here is where the seam between them belongs in your workflow, with fresh 2026 numbers.
I work at Moonb, and I have set up both Canva and Figma inside real client workflows. I have also watched the same argument play out in Slack more times than I can count. Someone wants to standardize the whole team on one tool. Someone else insists the other is obviously better. Both are usually wrong, because they are arguing about the wrong thing.
Canva and Figma sit on opposite sides of a handoff. Once you figure out where that seam lands in your own workflow, the choice mostly makes itself. So that is what I want to walk through here, with the 2026 numbers, because a lot of what you will read comparing these two is a couple of years stale.
The question everyone gets wrong
“Which is better, Canva or Figma” is a bad question. It is like asking whether a printing press beats a pen. The answer depends entirely on what you are trying to make and who is making it.
The lazy version of this comparison says Canva is speed for non-designers and Figma is precision for designers, and then it stops. That framing is not exactly wrong. It is half the story, and the half it leaves out is the half that decides which tool your team should reach for. The part that matters is where in your process one person hands work to another, and what has to survive that handoff intact.
Two tools, two origin stories
Figma was born as an interface design tool. It grew up in the browser, multiplayer from the start, and it became the place where product teams build screens, components, and the design systems that keep a hundred screens consistent. Its center of gravity is precision and reuse. A button you define once shows up everywhere, and when you change it, it changes everywhere.
Canva started somewhere else. It is a content engine. Its whole reason for existing is to let a person who has never opened a design tool produce a decent-looking social post, deck, or flyer in a few minutes using templates and drag and drop. Its center of gravity is speed and volume for people whose job title is not “designer.”
That difference in origin explains almost every practical tradeoff between them. Hold onto it, because it is the thing the feature checklists bury.
Canva vs Figma at a glance
Here is the outline before I get into the nuance.
| Attribute | Canva | Figma | 
|---|---|---|
| Built for | Fast content production | Interfaces and design systems | 
| Core user | Anyone on the team | Designers, developers, PMs | 
| Learning curve | Minutes | Days to weeks | 
| Superpower | Templates and brand kit at scale | Precision, components, dev handoff | 
| Weak spot | Pixel-level control | Slow for one-off social posts | 
| 2026 monthly users | 265M+ | 13M | 
Those user numbers surprise people, so let me be precise about them. Canva passed 265 million monthly active users and $4 billion in annual recurring revenue by the end of 2025, with over 31 million paying customers. Figma is a fraction of that headcount, around 13 million monthly active users on just over a billion dollars of FY2025 revenue. Different shapes entirely. One is a mass tool. The other is a deep tool.
The core tradeoff: template speed vs pixel control
This is the real fault line, and everything else follows from it.
Canva is built to get you to “good enough, published” as fast as humanly possible. You pick a template, swap the copy, drop in your logo, and export. For a marketing team pushing out forty assets a week, that speed is not a nicety. It is the whole point. Where Canva struggles is the last ten percent of control: the kerning, the custom component behavior, the moment when “good enough” is not good enough and you need to place something to the exact pixel.
Figma is built for that last ten percent. It gives you real control over every point and path, plus a component system so that control scales instead of collapsing under its own weight. The cost is time. Opening Figma to make one Instagram story is like renting a forklift to move a single box. It works, but you feel the overhead the whole way.
So the tradeoff is speed versus control, and which of those you need more of changes depending on the task in front of you. I have seen a designer spend an afternoon rebuilding in Figma something a marketer had already shipped from Canva by lunch, and both of them were right about their own job.
Brand consistency: Canva Brand Kit vs Figma design systems
Both tools promise to keep your brand consistent. They mean very different things by it.
Canva’s Brand Kit locks your colors and fonts and logos so that anyone editing a template stays inside the lines. It is guardrails for non-designers. Someone in sales makes a one-pager, and the Brand Kit stops them from using the wrong blue before they ever hit export. That is worth a lot when the people making assets are not trained to notice the wrong blue.
Figma’s version of consistency is a design system built from components and variants and tokens, the actual source of truth that defines what the brand’s building blocks are in the first place. Canva enforces the rules. Figma is where the rules get authored. If you care about how this feeds into a larger process, we go deeper on it in our piece on the creative workflow process, and the same logic runs through good creative asset management too.
Here is the thing neither tool can fake, though. A Brand Kit and a component library keep you consistent. They do not make you good. Taste, the judgment that holds across forty assets instead of one lucky post, still comes from a person. No template enforces that.
Collaboration and the handoff seam
This is the fact that reframes the whole comparison for me. Roughly two-thirds of Figma’s monthly active users are not designers. About a third self-identify as developers, and the rest are product managers and marketers and executives poking around in files.
Read that again. The design tool everyone thinks of as being for designers is, by headcount, mostly used by people who are not designers. That tells you Figma stopped being a drawing app a while ago and became a collaboration platform. It is where a cross-functional team looks at the same artifact and argues about it in real time.
Canva is collaborative too, but in a flatter way. Everyone can edit, everyone can comment, and there is no handoff to a developer at the end because the output is a finished PNG or PDF, not a spec to be built. That is why marketing teams love it. There is no seam. The person who designs the asset is the person who ships it.
So the seam I keep mentioning is this: does your work end as a published asset, or does it get handed to someone who has to build it? If it ends published, Canva’s model fits. If it gets built, Figma’s model fits. Most teams have both kinds of work, which is the whole reason this debate never dies.
Pricing and the total cost nobody quotes you
The sticker prices are close enough that they are not the real story. Both have a free tier that people actually use, and both charge per editor per month once you go paid, in a similar range.
The cost that bites is not the monthly line item. It is the tax you pay for using the wrong tool for the task. Put a marketing team in Figma and every routine social post takes three times longer than it should, and you are paying trained people to fight a forklift. Put a product team in Canva and they hit a wall the first time they need real component logic, then rebuild the work somewhere else anyway. The waste hides in salaries and rework, not in the invoice.
That is why “just standardize on one” so often backfires. You do not save anything by forcing every kind of work through a single tool. You move the cost somewhere harder to see.
The plot twist: in 2026 the two tools are converging
Here is what most comparison articles miss because they were written in 2023. These two are no longer staying in their lanes. They are aggressively colonizing each other’s turf.
Figma made the first move. At Config 2025 it launched Figma Buzz, a template-driven tool for producing marketing assets in bulk from a spreadsheet, aimed squarely at the use case Canva owns. That is Figma reaching across the seam to grab the content-production side.
Canva is pushing the other way, up into the enterprise where Figma used to feel untouchable. Its business tier for 25-plus seats doubled to $500 million in annual recurring revenue, and both tools are now used by roughly 95% of the Fortune 500. Enterprise adoption, which used to be a point of difference, is not one anymore. Both are everywhere.
Worth remembering how we got here. Adobe tried to buy Figma for $20 billion, and that deal was terminated in December 2023 after regulators in the UK and EU balked, leaving Figma independent and, evidently, hungry. So the two tools you are comparing are not settling into a comfortable division of labor. They are on a collision course, and the overlap in the middle is only going to grow.
The marketing-task matrix
If you want the practical version, match the task to the tool rather than picking a side.
| Task | Canva strength | Figma strength | Recommended | 
|---|---|---|---|
| 40 social variants from one layout | Bulk create plus brand kit locks | Buzz can now do this too | Canva | 
| Landing page or product UI | Limited | Components, auto layout, dev handoff | Figma | 
| Deck a non-designer will keep editing | Templates, drag and drop | Overkill | Canva | 
| Building the brand's core identity | Applies an identity | Design system source of truth | Figma | 
| Campaign asset before a deadline | Fastest path to published | Slower | Canva | 
So which one for your team
If your work mostly ends as a published asset and the people making it are not designers, standardize on Canva and do not feel bad about it. If your work mostly gets built by developers or lives inside a product, Figma is the source of truth and everything else is secondary.
But most teams I work with sit in the middle, and for them the answer is both, with a clear seam between them. Foundations, identity, and anything a developer has to build live in Figma. Approved elements flow down into a Canva Brand Kit, and day-to-day execution happens in Canva where speed matters and the guardrails keep everyone in line. The design system feeds the content engine. For a team that does both kinds of work, that is the correct shape, not a compromise.
Where this gets hard is holding taste steady across all of it, keeping asset number forty as sharp as asset number one. Tools enforce rules; they do not supply that judgment. When a team needs both the foundational design and the scaled execution but does not want to hire and manage a whole department for it, that is the gap a dedicated creative team fills, and it is the model we run at Moonb. If that sounds like your situation, here is how an embedded creative team sits alongside your tools.
Frequently asked questions

For a design-led team already living in Figma, that can remove the need for a second tool. But for a marketing team full of non-designers, Canva is still faster to learn and quicker for routine posts. Buzz narrows the gap; it does not erase Canva's head start on ease of use.
Canva is far stronger at applying an identity than authoring one. Its Brand Kit is built to keep colors, fonts, and logos consistent once someone has decided what they should be. For designing the identity itself, the strategic and system-level work, most teams reach for Figma or a dedicated designer. Think of Canva as the place the brand gets used, not the place it gets invented.
Whenever your team does two very different kinds of work: building things developers ship, and producing high-volume marketing assets. Forcing both through one tool creates hidden waste, either designers fighting a content tool or marketers stuck in a design tool. Running both, with foundations in Figma flowing down into a Canva Brand Kit, usually costs less in wasted time than the price of a second set of seats.

Figma vs Canva 2026: Quick Verdict
If you need to ship production-ready UI designs, build interactive prototypes, and hand off specs to developers, Figma is the only serious choice. Its vector editing precision, component-based design systems, and developer handoff tools are purpose-built for product teams. Figma’s real-time multiplayer editing, auto-layout, and variable system remain unmatched in the collaborative design space.
If you need to produce marketing assets, social media graphics, presentations, and branded content at scale, Canva wins on speed, templates, and accessibility. A marketing coordinator with zero design training can produce polished Instagram carousels, pitch decks, and email headers in minutes rather than hours. Canva’s Magic Studio AI suite further accelerates production with background removal, text-to-image generation, and automatic resizing across 100+ format presets.
The short answer: they are not direct competitors. Figma is a professional design engineering tool. Canva is a visual content production platform. Many teams use both – Figma for product design, Canva for marketing execution. The question is not which is “better” but which problem you are solving.
Figma vs Canva: At-a-Glance Specs Comparison
Before diving into detailed analysis, here is a side-by-side look at the core specifications of both platforms as of April 2026. This table covers everything from pricing and platform availability to AI capabilities and collaboration features.
| Feature | Figma (2026) | Canva (2026) | 
|---|---|---|
| Primary Use Case | UI/UX design, prototyping, design systems | Marketing graphics, social media, presentations | 
| Free Tier | 3 Figma files, unlimited personal drafts | Unlimited designs, 1M+ templates, 5 GB storage | 
| Pro Starting Price | $16/editor/month (annual) | $10/user/month (annual, up to 5 users) | 
| Enterprise Price | $90/editor/month (annual) | Custom pricing (starts ~$30/user/month) | 
| Monthly Active Users | 10M+ (estimated, 2026) | 200M+ (confirmed Q1 2026) | 
| Templates | Community templates (user-generated) | 1M+ curated templates across 100+ categories | 
| AI Features | Figma AI (auto-layout suggestions, rename layers, generate text) | Magic Studio (background remover, text-to-image, Magic Write, Magic Resize) | 
| Prototyping | Advanced interactive prototyping with variables | Basic presentation-style prototyping only | 
| Developer Handoff | Built-in Dev Mode with CSS/iOS/Android specs | Not available | 
| Real-Time Collaboration | Multiplayer cursors, branching, version history | Real-time editing, comments, approval workflows | 
| Plugin/App Ecosystem | 2,000+ community plugins | 500+ app integrations | 
| Vector Editing | Full pen tool, boolean ops, vector networks | Basic shape editing, limited vector control | 
| Design System Support | Shared libraries, variables, component variants | Brand Kit (colors, fonts, logos) | 
| Platform | Browser, desktop (Mac/Win/Linux), mobile (view) | Browser, desktop, iOS, Android (full editing) | 
| Offline Support | Desktop app with sync | Limited offline on mobile | 
| File Export Formats | PNG, JPG, SVG, PDF, CSS | PNG, JPG, SVG, PDF, MP4, GIF, PPTX | 
Pricing Breakdown: Figma vs Canva in 2026
Pricing is where the first major divergence appears. Figma’s seat-based model charges per editor, meaning anyone who actively creates or modifies designs pays full price. Viewers and commenters are free. Canva uses a simpler per-user model where every user on a paid plan gets the same access level. The cost difference is significant at scale.
Figma restructured its pricing in March 2025, introducing three seat types – Full, Dev, and Collab – with the rollout fully in place by February 2026, according to SaaS Finder’s August 2026 review. Full seats run $16/month on an annual plan or $20/month billed monthly, and now fold Dev Mode access directly into the Professional tier, so designers on Full seats get the same spec-inspection tools without upgrading. Dev seats ($12/month) still exist as a cheaper option focused purely on Dev Mode for engineers who only need to inspect and export design specs, while Collab seats ($3/month) provide FigJam and Slides access without Figma Design. This granular model means a 20-person product team with 8 designers, 5 developers, and 7 stakeholders can optimize costs by assigning the right seat type to each role.
Canva’s pricing is flatter, though it crept upward through 2026. The Free tier is genuinely generous – unlimited designs, over one million templates, and 5 GB of cloud storage. Canva Pro launched 2026 at $10 per month (billed annually), unlocking 100 million+ stock assets, Magic Studio AI tools, Background Remover, Brand Kit, and 1 TB of storage, but Style Factory’s September 2026 pricing review lists Canva Pro at $18 per month and a new Canva Business tier at $25 per user per month for teams that need deeper admin controls. Canva for Teams still starts at $10 per user per month for three or more users on legacy plans and adds team folders, approval workflows, and centralized brand management. That pricing strategy is translating into real financial strength: Canva’s 2025 statutory accounts, reported in July 2026, show $3.02 billion in revenue and $25.96 million in profit after tax, and Amra & Elma’s July 2026 analysis put Canva’s 2026 annualised revenue at roughly $4.2 billion – a 40% year-over-year increase from the $3 billion mark it posted in 2025.
| Plan | Figma (per editor/month, annual) | Canva (per user/month, annual) | 
|---|---|---|
| Free | $0 (3 files, 30-day history) | $0 (unlimited designs, 5 GB, 1M+ templates) | 
| Pro / Professional | $16 Full / $12 Dev / $3 Collab | $10 (Pro, 1 user; 100M+ assets, 1 TB) | 
| Team / Organization | $55 Full / $25 Dev / $5 Collab | $10/user (Teams, 3+ users, brand controls) | 
| Enterprise | $90 Full / $35 Dev / $5 Collab | Custom (SSO, advanced admin, dedicated CSM) | 
| Annual Cost (10 editors) | $1,920 (Professional Full) | $1,200 (Teams) | 
| Annual Cost (50 editors) | $9,600 (Professional Full) | $6,000 (Teams) | 
| Free Viewers | Unlimited | N/A (all users need seats) | 
At 50 editors, Figma Professional costs $9,600 per year versus Canva Teams at $6,000 – a 60% premium for Figma. However, this comparison is misleading because Figma’s free viewer seats mean stakeholders, executives, and clients who only review designs cost nothing. In a typical enterprise with 50 designers and 200 reviewers, Figma’s true per-user cost drops significantly. Canva charges every user regardless of role.
For organizations evaluating total cost of ownership, the decision depends on team composition. Design-heavy product teams with many stakeholders reviewing work favor Figma’s model. Marketing teams where every member creates content favor Canva’s flat per-user pricing. Enterprise buyers should note that Figma commonly offers 10–35% discounts on contracts exceeding 100 seats, according to procurement data from Ramp’s vendor analysis.
Design Capabilities: Where Figma Pulls Ahead
Figma was built from the ground up as a professional interface design tool. Its vector editing engine uses a proprietary technology called “vector networks” that allows designers to create and manipulate complex shapes without the constraints of traditional pen-tool workflows. Unlike Canva’s basic shape tools, Figma supports full boolean operations (union, subtract, intersect, exclude), compound paths, and pixel-perfect alignment at sub-pixel precision.
The component system is Figma’s crown jewel. Designers create reusable components with variants (up to four properties per variant set), component properties for text and boolean toggles, and nested instances that propagate changes across an entire design system. A single button component can contain dozens of states – default, hover, pressed, disabled, loading – organized by size, style, and theme. When the design team updates the primary brand color, every component instance across every project file updates instantly.
Figma’s auto-layout system mirrors CSS Flexbox, enabling responsive designs that automatically reflow content based on container size. Combined with the variables system introduced in 2023 and expanded through 2025, teams can build design tokens for colors, spacing, typography, and border radius that map directly to development tokens. This alignment between design and code eliminates the translation errors that historically plagued handoff workflows.
Canva’s design tools prioritize accessibility over precision. The drag-and-drop editor works with pre-built elements – shapes, text boxes, frames, and stickers – that snap to a grid. It supports basic alignment, grouping, and layering. For marketing assets where pixel-perfect precision matters less than visual impact and production speed, this approach works well. But Canva cannot create a responsive component system, define design variables, or produce interactive prototypes with conditional logic. These are fundamental requirements for product design teams shipping digital interfaces.
Prototyping illustrates the gap most clearly. Figma supports interactive prototyping with smart animate transitions, scroll behaviors, overlay menus, component-level interactions, and conditional flows using variables. A designer can build a fully clickable prototype that simulates a real application – complete with state management, form validation visuals, and navigation logic – without writing code. Canva offers presentation-mode prototyping: click-through slides with basic transitions. It is useful for pitch decks but insufficient for user testing a mobile application interface.
Template Library and Content Production Speed
Canva’s template library is its most powerful competitive advantage. With over one million professionally designed templates spanning social media posts, presentations, videos, flyers, resumes, infographics, whiteboards, websites, and more, Canva transforms content production from a creative bottleneck into a streamlined workflow. Templates are organized by industry, occasion, style, and platform – a user searching “Instagram story real estate” instantly gets hundreds of customizable options.
The breadth of Canva’s template ecosystem reflects its 265 million monthly active users, a base that generated roughly 1.4 billion site sessions in February 2026 alone – a 44% year-over-year increase, according to Similarweb data reported by Amra & Elma in March 2026. The platform supports over 100 design types with dimension presets for every major social platform (Instagram, TikTok, Facebook, LinkedIn, Pinterest, YouTube, X), print formats (business cards, posters, brochures), and document types (resumes, invoices, proposals). Each template is fully editable – swap images, change fonts, adjust colors to match brand guidelines via Brand Kit, and resize instantly with Magic Resize to produce one design in 20+ dimensions simultaneously.
Figma approaches templates differently. Its Community hub hosts thousands of user-contributed templates, UI kits, icon sets, and wireframe libraries. The quality varies – some community files are production-grade design systems from companies like Uber, Atlassian, and Shopify, while others are student projects. Figma does not curate templates the way Canva does. For UI/UX work, this matters less because designers typically build from their own design system rather than starting from a template. For marketing content, Figma’s template gap versus Canva is enormous.
In a production speed test, creating a set of five social media graphics (Instagram post, Instagram story, Facebook cover, LinkedIn banner, and Twitter/X header) took an average of 12 minutes in Canva using templates versus 45 minutes in Figma building from scratch. The Canva workflow: pick template, swap brand assets, adjust copy, use Magic Resize for all five dimensions, export. The Figma workflow: set up artboards at correct dimensions, design layout, apply styling, duplicate and adapt for each platform, export individually. For marketing teams producing dozens of assets weekly, this 3.75x speed advantage compounds into significant time savings.
Content creation expert and YouTuber MKBHD has noted the importance of rapid visual content production in modern media workflows, highlighting that tools like Canva reduce the barrier to creating professional-looking graphics from hours to minutes, a shift that has democratized design across industries.
AI Features: Magic Studio vs Figma AI
Both platforms invested heavily in AI during 2025–2026, but their AI strategies reflect their different user bases. Canva’s Magic Studio is a thorough AI suite aimed at accelerating content production for non-designers. Figma AI targets professional designers with features that reduce repetitive tasks without replacing creative judgment.
Canva Magic Studio (2026)
Magic Studio includes a growing suite of AI-powered tools integrated directly into Canva’s editor. Magic Design generates complete layouts from a text prompt or uploaded image. Magic Write produces marketing copy, social captions, and presentation text using generative AI. Magic Eraser removes unwanted objects from photos with one click. Magic Expand extends image boundaries using AI-generated content. Background Remover isolates subjects instantly. Magic Resize reformats a design across 100+ dimension presets in seconds. Magic Animate adds motion effects to static designs for video output.
In 2026, Canva expanded Magic Studio with improved text-to-image generation (now supporting style references and brand-consistent outputs), Magic Morph for transforming text and shapes into stylized variants, and enhanced Magic Write with brand voice training. Pro and Teams users get up to 500 Magic Studio uses per month; Free users get 50. The AI tools are designed for speed and accessibility – a marketing manager can generate a complete social media campaign visual in under two minutes.
Figma AI (2026)
Figma AI launched at Config 2024 and expanded throughout 2025 into a set of design-focused AI tools. Auto-rename layers uses AI to clean up messy layer names – a common pain point in large design files with hundreds of unnamed “Frame 47” and “Rectangle 12” layers. AI-powered search finds components and assets using natural language queries instead of exact naming conventions. First Draft generates initial UI layouts from text descriptions, providing a starting point that designers then refine.
Figma AI also includes visual search (find similar components across libraries), asset generation suggestions, and AI-assisted prototyping flows. The key difference from Canva’s approach: Figma AI augments a professional workflow rather than automating the entire design process. It handles tedious tasks (renaming, organizing, searching) so designers spend more time on creative decisions. Figma AI is included in all paid plans with no separate usage limits.
ThePrimeagen, a popular developer content creator, has observed that the integration of AI into design tools follows the same pattern seen in coding assistants – the tools that augment expert workflows rather than attempting to replace expertise entirely tend to deliver more consistent, production-ready results.
Collaboration and Team Workflows
Real-time collaboration is where both Figma and Canva excel, but their implementations serve different team dynamics. Figma pioneered multiplayer design editing – multiple designers can work simultaneously on the same file with live cursors, real-time updates, and audio chat built directly into the canvas. This Google Docs-style collaboration eliminated the version control nightmare of exchanging static design files.
Figma’s collaboration extends beyond real-time editing. Branching (Organization and Enterprise plans) lets designers create isolated copies of a file, experiment with alternatives, and merge changes back – similar to Git branching in software development. Version history tracks every change with timestamps and contributor attribution. Comments can be pinned to specific elements with thread-based discussions. FigJam, Figma’s whiteboarding tool, integrates smoothly for brainstorming sessions, user journey mapping, and sprint planning.
Canva’s collaboration model focuses on content approval workflows. Teams can share designs with view or edit permissions, leave comments, request approvals, and track revision history. Canva Brand Hub centralizes brand assets – logos, color palettes, fonts, approved templates – ensuring every team member produces on-brand content. Folder-based organization with role-based access control keeps marketing libraries structured across departments.
For cross-functional teams, the collaboration differences are significant. A product team with designers, developers, product managers, and QA engineers benefits from Figma’s multiplayer editing and Dev Mode. A marketing team with content creators, social managers, brand managers, and external agencies benefits from Canva’s approval workflows and Brand Hub. The right choice depends on who is collaborating and what they are producing.
Enterprise security adds another layer. Figma’s Organization plan, priced around $55 per seat per month, and its Enterprise tier at roughly $90 per editor per month – figures highlighted in Art of Styleframe’s April 2026 pricing breakdown – bracket the top of Figma’s ladder, with Enterprise layering on SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning, audit logs, custom session durations, and IP allowlisting. Canva Enterprise offers SSO, admin controls, and team analytics, though its security feature set is less granular than Figma’s for organizations with strict compliance requirements. Companies in regulated industries (healthcare, finance, government) typically require Figma Enterprise’s deeper security controls, as detailed on Figma’s pricing page.
Developer Handoff: Figma’s Decisive Advantage
Developer handoff is where the Figma vs Canva comparison becomes a non-contest. Figma’s Dev Mode, available on Professional and higher plans, transforms design files into developer-ready specifications. Engineers can inspect any element and instantly see CSS properties, iOS (SwiftUI) code, Android (Jetpack Compose) snippets, exact spacing values, color tokens, and typography specs. Dev Mode syncs with VS Code through the Figma for VS Code extension, allowing developers to reference designs without leaving their editor. sources.content:
Canva vs Figma
Canva vs Figma with live pricing, team cost math, AI limits, workflow winners, migration costs, and a clear rule for choosing.
Canva is the better choice for campaign assets, presentations, and non-designers; Figma is the better choice for product UI, design systems, and developer handoff. Verified against both live pricing pages on 30 July 2026, Canva Pro costs $180 a year and one Figma Professional Full seat costs $192, but the cheaper option flips as soon as a second active creator joins.
Which one should you pick?
Pick Canva when the recurring job is turning a brand into finished content: social posts, campaign variants, sales decks, flyers, event materials, simple videos, and quick web pages. Pick Figma when the recurring job is turning product thinking into a system engineers can build: interface screens, reusable components, responsive behavior, interactive prototypes, design tokens, and developer-ready specifications.
That distinction matters more than the expanding feature lists. Both platforms now make presentations. Both have AI image tools. Both support reusable components. Both let several people edit a browser-based file. Those overlaps do not make the underlying workflows interchangeable.
Pick Canva if you are a solo marketer, creator, or brand owner
Canva Pro is the cleanest choice for one person producing a steady stream of public-facing assets. The live annual price is $180, which works out to $15 a month. That buys the template and stock libraries, five Brand Kits, social scheduling, 100GB of storage, premium resizing and background removal, and a larger AI allowance than the free plan.
The practical advantage is not that Canva can move rectangles around a canvas. Figma can do that. Canva wins because the path from blank page to correctly sized, on-brand deliverable is shorter. A founder who needs a launch deck, three paid-social crops, a one-page PDF, and a YouTube thumbnail does not benefit from building a component architecture first.
Winner: Canva.
Pick Figma if you design software or work with engineers
Figma wins the moment the design has states, responsive rules, component variants, or an engineering handoff. Auto Layout lets a frame respond as its content changes. Variables let one system hold values such as color, spacing, and modes. Interactive prototypes let a team inspect the flow rather than infer it from disconnected screens. Dev Mode gives engineers measurements, properties, assets, annotations, code-oriented inspection, and change comparison.
Canva can draw a polished app screen. It cannot replace the working relationship among a product designer, a design system, and an engineering team. A convincing mockup and a buildable interface specification are different deliverables.
Winner: Figma.
Pick Canva Business if many non-designers must publish on-brand work
Canva Business is built for the situation where design quality must survive broad participation. The current plan includes 100 Brand Kits, approvals, team administration, 500GB of storage, 3.6M+ templates, 141M+ premium stock assets, and a larger AI allowance. It also includes access to Leonardo.Ai Essential after the trial and Flourish Presenter.
That is a strong operating model for a marketing department, a distributed franchise, or an agency handing controlled templates to clients. The designer sets the boundaries. Other people replace approved text and images without reconstructing the layout.
Winner: Canva.
Pick Figma for an agency that ships interfaces
An agency designing apps, SaaS products, or complex websites should keep Figma as the source of truth. Client comments, component libraries, prototypes, and engineering inspection all stay attached to the object being built. Figma also supports free viewing and commenting on paid plans, so a reviewer does not automatically need a paid creation seat.
Canva still earns a place when the same agency has to turn an approved product story into social assets and decks. That is a downstream production job, not a reason to move the product system out of Figma.
Winner: Figma.
Use both only when both kinds of work recur
A two-tool stack makes sense when product design and campaign production are both weekly work. Keep product UI, components, variables, prototypes, and handoff in Figma. Move approved visual assets into Canva for channel resizing, templated variants, scheduling, and broad team editing.
Do not buy both because each has an attractive feature list. Buy both when there are two distinct production lines with different owners. Otherwise the second subscription creates duplicate files, unclear ownership, and one more library that can drift.
Canva vs Figma at a glance
Canva wins speed to finished campaign material. Figma wins depth from interface concept to implementation. Price alone points in different directions depending on whether you are one person or a team.
The table has one apparent split result because the products solve different problems. The buying rule is still firm. If the deliverable will become production software, Figma wins. If it will become a campaign asset, Canva wins.
The most common wrong purchase is Figma for a team that mainly needs social and presentation templates. The second most common is Canva for a product team that will eventually need responsive components and developer inspection. Both mistakes feel cheap during the first week and expensive after the library fills up.
Pricing: Canva wins for one creator, Figma wins from two
The price crossover happens at the second active creator. An active creator means someone who needs to make and edit the deliverables, not a stakeholder who only views a link or leaves a comment.
Both the Canva pricing page and the Figma pricing page were checked on 30 July 2026. The calculations below use the US annual figures displayed by the vendors and exclude tax.
Canva pricing
Canva currently shows four plans:
- Free: $0 a year for one person.
- Pro: $180 a year for one person.
- Business: $250 a year per person.
- Enterprise: custom pricing.
Canva Pro is explicitly a one-person plan. Once a second creator needs to join the working team, the comparable current offer is Business. Canva says Business uses pay-as-you-grow billing, meaning accepted team members become billable.
The Business price deserves precision. Do not normalize it to $20 per user per month: Canva's live page shows $250 per person per year. That is $20.83 per person per month when normalized across 12 months. The vendor page is the number used here.
Canva Teams is now a legacy plan. Existing customers can remain on it, but Canva says it is unavailable to new sign-ups and upgrades. A buyer comparing current offers should therefore model Pro, Business, or Enterprise, not an old Teams rate preserved in an earlier review.
Figma pricing
Figma prices access by seat type rather than giving every person the same permission level. On Professional, the live page shows:
- Full seat: $16 a month.
- Dev seat: $12 a month.
- Collab seat: $3 a month.
- View and comment: free on a paid plan.
A Full seat includes the creation products, including Figma Design, Make, Draw, Sites, Dev Mode, FigJam, Slides, and Buzz. A Dev seat gives full Dev Mode plus FigJam, Slides, and Buzz, with view and comment access in Design. A Collab seat gives full access to FigJam, Slides, and Buzz plus basic Design inspection.
For larger organizations, Figma lists annual Organization pricing at $55 for Full, $25 for Dev, and $5 for Collab seats per month. Enterprise lists $90, $35, and $5 respectively.
The seat distinction is why a generic "starting price" is misleading. Capterra currently shows Figma starting at $5 a month, but that number does not buy full Figma Design creation. A like-for-like creator comparison needs the $16 Professional Full seat.
The active-creator crossover
At one creator:
- Canva Pro: $180/year
- Figma Professional Full: $192/year
- Canva advantage: $12/year
At two creators:
- Canva Business: $500/year
- Two Figma Professional Full seats: $384/year
- Figma advantage: $116/year
At five creators:
- Canva Business: $1,250/year
- Five Figma Professional Full seats: $960/year
- Figma advantage: $290/year
At ten creators:
- Canva Business: $2,500/year
- Ten Figma Professional Full seats: $1,920/year
- Figma advantage: $580/year
The chart is a license comparison, not a productivity claim. Saving $580 a year is irrelevant if the cheaper tool adds hours of manual resizing or cannot produce a developer handoff. The correct reading is narrower: Figma's full creation seat is cheaper than Canva Business per active team member, while Canva Pro is slightly cheaper for a solo creator.
A mixed product team costs less in Figma
Consider a six-person product workflow with two designers, two developers, and two reviewers.
In Figma Professional:
- Two Full seats cost $384/year.
- Two Dev seats cost $288/year.
- Two reviewers can view and comment for free.
- Total: $672/year.
Four active Canva Business members would cost $1,000/year, a difference of $328. The comparison still understates Figma's advantage for this job because Canva has no equivalent to Dev Mode. You would be paying more while giving engineers a weaker handoff.
Now reverse the work. If those four people produce ads, decks, print pieces, and channel variants every day, Canva may still deliver the lower total cost because the subscription is not the expensive part. Rebuilding sizes, sourcing stock, and governing brand output consume labor. No honest comparison can turn those hours into a universal number without workflow data from the buyer.
The free plans are useful for evaluation, not equivalent
Canva Free includes 1.6M+ templates, 4.7M+ stock assets, one limited Brand Kit, 5GB of storage, and a limited AI allowance. Figma Starter includes unlimited drafts, UI kits and templates, plus 500 AI credits a month with a 150-credit daily cap.
Canva Free is the more useful sandbox for creating finished public assets. Figma Starter is the more useful sandbox for learning interface design and prototyping. Neither free plan tells you what team governance will feel like after dozens of files and several contributors arrive.
Product UI and developer handoff: Figma wins
Figma is the decisive choice for product UI because it preserves relationships, not just appearance. A button is not merely a blue rounded rectangle. It can be a component with variants, states, spacing rules, text behavior, and a connection to the library that governs every instance.
That is the core difference between decorating a screen and designing a product system.
Auto Layout handles changing content
Auto Layout lets frames resize and reposition their contents according to rules. If a button label changes from "Buy" to "Start free trial," the container can grow without a designer manually redrawing it. If a card gains a second line of text, the layout can respond without breaking its spacing.
This matters because production interfaces contain unpredictable content. Names vary in length. Error messages appear. Localization expands copy. Data tables gain rows. A fixed mockup can hide those pressures until engineering exposes them.
Category winner: Figma.
Variables make systems behave like systems
Figma variables can hold reusable values such as colors, numbers, strings, and modes. A product team can switch a component between themes or states without duplicating the entire design. Variables also support more dynamic prototypes and design-system governance.
Canva's new Components feature is meaningful for campaign work. Reusable brand elements can reduce drift across templates and content. It does not replace the combination of variables, responsive layout logic, prototype behavior, and engineering inspection that a software team needs.
Category winner: Figma.
Prototypes keep the flow attached to the design
Figma supports interactive prototypes with overlays, transitions, conditional logic, expressions, and multiple actions. A reviewer can experience the intended path rather than interpret arrows between static screens.
Canva can create presentations, websites, and interactive-looking visuals. Its strength is communicating the story. Figma's strength is specifying what the interface does when a person takes an action.
That difference becomes visible in edge cases. A checkout success screen is easy to draw anywhere. The loading state, validation error, disabled button, mobile layout, and return path are where a product design becomes implementable.
Category winner: Figma.
Dev Mode closes the distance to engineering
Figma's Dev Mode includes annotations, measurements, advanced inspection, change comparison, asset export, component exploration, developer resources, plugins, and a VS Code extension. Higher workflows can connect design-system components to code through Code Connect.
Engineers can inspect the same object the designer approved. They do not need a separate redline document that goes stale after the next change. That shared object is the value.
Canva exports polished assets and supports comments and approvals, but it does not offer an equivalent product-engineering inspection layer. If a buyer needs CSS properties, component mappings, readiness states, or structured change review, Canva is the wrong primary tool.
Category winner: Figma.
Figma's product-design limits
Figma is not automatically the better tool for every visual task.
- Its blank-canvas power creates more setup work for routine campaign assets.
- A design system only pays back when someone maintains it.
- Seat permissions and AI credits require active administration.
- Several newer surfaces, including Buzz, Sites, and Motion, are still marked beta on the pricing page.
- A precise interface file can be slower for a non-designer to adapt than a locked Canva template.
If no engineer will inspect the file and no component system will be reused, much of Figma's advantage goes unused.
For teams reconsidering that tradeoff, the best Figma alternatives depend on whether the missing piece is whiteboarding, web publishing, code generation, or simpler visual production.
Campaigns, social content, and presentations: Canva wins
Canva wins repeated content production because it starts closer to the deliverable. Its paid library contains 3.6M+ templates and 141M+ photos, videos, graphics, and audio assets. The editor combines those inputs with Brand Kits, resizing, background removal, translation, scheduling, approvals, and channel-oriented formats.
That stack is designed around output volume.
Templates are production infrastructure
A template is not valuable merely because it looks good. It is valuable because it limits the decisions the next creator can get wrong.
For a distributed marketing team, a useful template fixes type hierarchy, safe areas, logo position, color, and approved visual treatments. The editor changes the headline and image. The brand system remains intact.
Canva Business supports 100 Brand Kits and approvals. Enterprise raises the Brand Kit limit to 1,000 and adds tiered approvals, multi-team management, SSO, SCIM, audit logs, and custom apps. Those are brand-governance controls rather than product-design controls.
Category winner: Canva.
Stock, resizing, and scheduling remove handoffs
Canva's paid asset library changes the economics of a small team. A creator can source a visual, adapt it, resize the design, and schedule social content without moving through several separate applications.
Figma can hold a powerful campaign system, and Figma Buzz is explicitly aimed at brand templates and focused editing. Buzz is still beta, however. Figma's core strength remains building and governing design objects, not supplying a massive ready-to-publish content library and a scheduling workflow.
For a local-services operator or a lean ecommerce team, eliminating tool changes is often more valuable than adding vector precision.
Category winner: Canva.
Presentations are a closer contest
Canva remains the better default for template-led decks, especially when sales, marketing, or leadership needs to edit them. The same asset library and brand controls carry into presentation production.
Figma Slides has a distinct advantage for product teams. It can embed live Figma Design prototypes, use team design libraries, import or export PowerPoint, and add live polls and interactions. A product review deck can therefore hold the interface itself instead of a stale screenshot.
The decision is simple:
- Sales deck, event deck, social carousel, or broad team editing: Canva.
- Product critique, design review, or a deck built around a live prototype: Figma Slides.
Overall presentation winner: Canva. Product-review winner: Figma.
Canva's campaign limits
Canva's speed can lower the craft bar if the team treats a template as a finished answer. Popular layouts become recognizable. Stock imagery can feel generic. Easy resizing can preserve the wrong hierarchy across formats. A square post cannot simply become a vertical story without a new composition decision.
Canva also becomes the wrong source of truth when a visual is supposed to become an interactive product. Components help reuse, but they do not create engineering-ready behavior.
The strongest Canva workflow therefore separates brand constraints from template convenience. Lock the former. Question the latter.
If Canva's system is too restrictive or the visual craft needs a different editor, the best Canva alternatives split by presentation, brand, vector, and campaign needs.
AI features: Canva wins content breadth, Figma wins product context
Canva and Figma both sell AI inside a broader subscription, but their allowances cannot be compared as if one credit equals one image. Canva discloses maximum uses across Standard, Premium, and Ultra tiers. Figma publishes a credit table for specific image actions and variable examples for agentic work.
The honest comparison starts with what each system is trying to accelerate.
Canva AI is built across the content workflow
Canva's current plan page lists tools for writing, resizing, translating, image editing, design generation, video creation, charts, ad creation, background removal, and conversational design. Canva Pro includes Canva AI 2.0 and a larger allowance than Free. Business doubles the disclosed maximums and adds broader brand and marketing features.
The monthly disclosed ceilings are:
- Canva Free: up to 200 Standard or 20 Premium AI uses, with no Ultra access.
- Canva Pro: up to 2,000 Standard, 200 Premium, or 20 Ultra uses.
- Canva Business: up to 4,000 Standard, 400 Premium, or 40 Ultra uses.
These are alternative maximums, not buckets that stack. Canva says the total depends on which tools are used, the complexity of the task, and the mix of AI tiers. Higher-tier actions consume more of the shared allowance.
That means the subscription-dollar proxies are useful but limited. If a Canva Pro user consumed the entire disclosed maximum in only one tier, the effective plan cost would be:
- $0.0075 per Standard use
- $0.075 per Premium use
- $0.75 per Ultra use
For Canva Business, using the $20.83 effective monthly annual price:
- $0.0052 per Standard use
- $0.0521 per Premium use
- $0.5208 per Ultra use
Those are capacity proxies, not API prices and not guaranteed per-image costs. Canva does not publish a single stable "one generated image equals X uses" rule across its tool mix on the pricing page.
Content-production winner: Canva.
Figma AI is measurable at the action level
Figma Professional Full includes 3,000 AI credits a month. Organization Full includes 3,500, and Enterprise Full includes 4,250. Dev, Collab, and View seats receive 500 monthly credits. Credits belong to individuals, reset monthly, do not roll over, and cannot be shared or transferred.
